item.title: Asylum applications drop 13% under EU migration pact
item.description:
Asylum applications drop 13% under EU migration pact

October 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of first-time asylum applications in the Netherlands fell by 13% in the third quarter of 2026, compared with the same period last year, according to figures from national statistics bureau CBS and immigration service IND.

The downward trend follows the implementation of the new European Union Migration Pact, which came into effect in June this year, with tighter guidelines, the abolition of permanent asylum residence permits and stricter criteria for family reunification.

Several of those changes echo measures pushed by former asylum minister Marjolein Faber (PVV), who promised the “strictest asylum policy ever” and wanted to make the Netherlands “as unattractive as possible to asylum seekers”. Her emergency asylum law was rejected by the Senate in April.

In the third quarter of 2026, some 5,900 people filed an asylum application for the first time, 850 fewer than a year earlier. Asylum applications from Eritreans and Syrians halved, while 1,500 fewer family reunification applicants came to the country than a year ago.

Eritreans submitted the most asylum claims, followed closely by Syrians. According to CBS, the number of Ukrainian applications increased from 15 to 140, while the number of applications from people from Ethiopia decreased from 290 to 75.

item.title: MPs call for ban on generative AI in primary schools
item.description:
MPs call for ban on generative AI in primary schools

October 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

MPs are calling for a ban on AI tools in Dutch primary schools, saying they threaten children’s ability to develop basic reading, writing and critical thinking skills.

A motion put forward by pan-European progressive party Volt and centrist Christian Democrat CDA asks the cabinet to arrange a formal rule disallowing tools like ChatGPT for primary school pupils. So far the motion has the backing of 10 parties with 88 of parliament’s 150 seats, according to broadcaster NOS.

Volt leader Laurens Dassen said in a statement: “I believe in the opportunities AI offers us, but at the same time generative AI is widening learning gaps.”

New learning goals for primary schools, due to take effect in 2027, will require pupils to explore AI and learn to “interact responsibly with an AI system”. In secondary school, students will start experimenting with training AI systems.

The motion tabled by Volt and CDA acknowledges these plans, and doesn’t rule out teaching children about AI, even if they wouldn’t be allowed to use it themselves.

Barend Last, an education specialist who teaches the final year of primary school, told NOS he agreed children should not have unlimited access to AI. However, he also said it can be a useful teaching tool if used in the right way, and that ruling it out altogether risks children learning too little about it.

The PO-Raad, the umbrella body for primary schools, said early research shows pupils learn less when they use generative AI heavily, and that it understood MPs’ concerns. But it said a total ban would come “out of the blue”, and that it would rather reach agreement with the education ministry.

item.title: Cabinet gathers to weigh right-wing bloc’s new joint demands
item.description:
Cabinet gathers to weigh right-wing bloc’s new joint demands

October 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Top members of the Dutch cabinet have gathered to discuss demands made on Thursday by a newly formed alliance of right-wing parties that could determine the future of the government’s tax plan.

On Thursday morning, leaders of the far-right JA21, orthodox Protestant party SGP, and farmer-citizen movement BBB announced they are banding together to force concessions in the tax plan negotiations.

They set out their demands – mainly concerning asylum, nitrogen and abortion – in a letter to the cabinet on Wednesday evening.

If their demands are met, the group says, it will support the cabinet on the rest of the tax plan and take a “constructive” approach to the budget.

The parties want to scrap plans to raise taxes to fund defence spending for NATO, as well as a planned VAT rise on flowers, and they want profit exemptions for small businesses raised.

Adjustments to the nitrogen plans demanded by BBB, harsher measures against asylum by JA21, and a pause on late-term abortions, home abortions and surrogacy demanded by the SGP are now joint demands by all three parties.

The move makes prime minister Jetten’s plans for broad support in which parties across the political spectrum back his plans, even more unlikely.

So far, opposition parties on the left and the right have said the coalition must choose a direction: side with left-wing parties like PRO and Volt, or with the right wing. Within the coalition, D66 and CDA prefer the former option, but the VVD has been leaning rightwards.

The letter contains a number of potentially intractable policies. Ending an obligation to the so-called “spreading law”, which requires all councils to house a fair share of asylum seekers, is something asylum minister Bart van den Brink (CDA) has said he cannot commit to.

Dropping the defence tax is particularly sensitive for the CDA. The SGP’s demands on abortion and surrogacy will clash with D66’s stances, broadcaster NOS reported.

The nitrogen proposals also conflict with agreements the cabinet has said are needed to get permits issued again, and PRO has said it will withdraw its support if the nitrogen plans are substantially changed.

item.title: Foreign residents: get organised, starting with dual nationality
item.description:
Foreign residents: get organised, starting with dual nationality

October 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Eelco Keij founded the Foundation for Dutch Nationals Abroad (SNBN), which lobbies for Dutch people living overseas. A bill due before parliament in December would allow dual nationality both for them and for foreign residents who naturalise here – but the coalition agreement only backs the first part. Keij says the international community needs to organise and lobby for itself, or risk being left behind.

Foreign residents in the Netherlands need lasting political influence, and could learn from another group that once had no voice in Dutch politics: Dutch citizens abroad.

In 2011, when I became a US citizen alongside my native Dutch citizenship, I realised that most Dutch people abroad could not have dual citizenship. As my case fell under one of the exceptions, I actually could be both. I felt lucky for myself, and pity for others. This is where my second realisation came in, possibly spurred by having worked for years in lobbying, advocacy and the Dutch parliament: no one in the Dutch political system would ever stand up for people like me, living abroad.

First, I set up a debate on dual nationality, from New York, and soon after, a petition among the Dutch abroad, reaching both astonishing numbers of citizens and articles in the Dutch national press. Aiming for a longer-term strategy, I studied how other European countries treated their citizens abroad. It turned out that in some countries the diaspora had organized itself in interest organisations, like the French, Danish and Swiss abroad.

Through this research, it became clear to me that the Dutch living abroad also needed a formal vehicle to be heard in Dutch politics. Together with other concerned Dutch citizens living abroad I founded the Foundation for the Dutch Abroad (SNBN), in 2019. The SNBN is a volunteer advocacy and lobby organization – strategic by design, focused on results.

Gaining recognition 
Aware that the Dutch political scene is fragmented, coalition-based, and unpredictable, our board is mostly formed of Dutch citizens abroad who are members of different political parties. That way, while remaining non-partisan as an organisation, board members have many formal and informal contacts with different political parties. As a consequence, Dutch politicians started hearing us, and seeing us.

Our efforts contributed to the 2022 constitutional change enabling Dutch citizens abroad to participate in elections for the Dutch Senate through an electoral college. Moreover, we saw how our outreach on various occasions led to mitigation of legislation and a willingness among Dutch politicians to engage with us, having discovered a new electorate.

Currently, we are fully focused on the advancement of a bill that was introduced almost ten years ago, which lies at the very heart of our foundation: allowing Dutch citizens abroad to have dual citizenship.

But the dual citizenship bill also covers foreigners in the Netherlands. If passed in full, it would also scrap the requirement forcing them to give up their original nationality.

Spoiler: that is not going to happen. The SNBN found there is currently no political majority to support foreigners in the Netherlands in their quest for dual citizenship. Their interests are beyond our mandate. But the political end result may be favoring the Dutch abroad, without equivalent progress for foreigners residing in the Netherlands – an aspect that could be dropped from the bill.

Time to start lobbying 
To our surprise, we have not seen a visible, coordinated lobby on behalf of foreign residents in the Netherlands in the debate on dual citizenship. The bill also covers them, yet they have been largely absent from the debate. So what to do now?

Unlike in countries such as Germany, Luxembourg and Ireland, where migrant-representing organizations already exist, we have not encountered a comparable, visible lobby in this debate on behalf of foreign residents in the Netherlands.

Perhaps with a suggested blueprint of the SNBN at hand, it may well be up to someone, a foreigner residing in the Netherlands, or a group of them, to step up and say: “Let’s start working on that.” Surely there are many issues this interest organisation could work on, including citizenship and naturalisation, family reunification, political participation and voting rights. Above all, it would give foreign residents visibility with Dutch politicians.

As SNBN we can attest to one thing: an important part of lasting political influence is to embed different political streams within the organization’s structure, whether it’s volunteer staff, board members or advisory board members. With that, and the right commitment, there is a real opportunity to build lasting political influence.

Readers: your turn.

item.title: Shell rakes in $12B profit as Middle East war drives up prices
item.description:
Shell rakes in $12B profit as Middle East war drives up prices

October 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Oil and gas giant Shell has recorded $10.8 billion in adjusted quarterly profits – double what it made in the same period last year – as war in the Middle East boosts energy prices.

Since the US and Israel began attacking Iran this year, Shell’s fuel products have risen in value, largely due to strikes on competing refineries in the region that produce petrol and diesel.

The corporation, which moved its headquarters out of The Hague to London in 2022, made record profits after Russia invaded Ukraine the same year, and has seen profits surge again since the outbreak of war with Iran.

MPs have called for a windfall tax to prevent Shell or other energy conglomerates from profiting from geopolitical conflict.

Shell’s move to London makes placing a levy on the profits harder, however, and the European Commission has also ruled out an EU-wide windfall tax, saying it’s a matter for individual nations.

item.title: Police name Serbian suspects in Tefaf jewellery heist
item.description:
Police name Serbian suspects in Tefaf jewellery heist

October 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch police have published the names of the five Serbian people suspected of robbing the Tefaf art fair in Maastricht in 2022. The gang got away with roughly €40 million in goods, according to Europol.

The suspects, four men and one woman, are Aleksandar Cenic (50), Aleksandar Stojiljkovic (50), Dusko Dimitrijevic (50), Bratislav Stojanovic (41) and Ninoslava Jovic (41). Police believe they are in the Serbian city of Niš or near Belgrade.

The public prosecution service (OM) is offering €20,000 for tip-offs leading to the arrest of any member of the group, who have all been placed on Europol’s most wanted list and the Dutch national wanted list, the OM said on Thursday.

The Serbian government is refusing extradition requests, which is standard practice for its own citizens. Dutch police said they hope that naming them will lead to tips about their movements, so they can be traced and caught if they travel abroad.

Four of the thieves went into the art fair on June 28, 2022, smartly dressed and wearing caps and glasses to partially conceal their identities. Police later identified a woman as a fifth suspect.

They were reportedly armed with what looked like guns, and were seen smashing glass cabinets with sledgehammers and grabbing jewellery. Two of the men held bystanders back with their weapons, and the gang fled on electric scooters.

None were caught in the immediate aftermath. Some of the stolen diamonds have since been recovered in Hong Kong, Israel and Botswana.

The fair’s insurer is also offering a reward of €500,000, broadcaster NOS reported.

item.title: Four women on trial after séance at Dutch cemetery
item.description:
Four women on trial after séance at Dutch cemetery

October 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Four women went on trial in a Utrecht court earlier this week for desecrating children’s graves during a séance they held at Amersfoort’s Rusthof Cemetery five years ago.

Prosecutors have demanded community service sentences of up to 200 hours for the women, who were trying to contact the dead after hours during a paranormal gathering. Two others with them, who are said only to have observed the ritual, are not being charged.

The cemetery’s director at the time was fired for giving the women permission to conduct research into the “so-called energies of the deceased” after closing time. The parents of children buried there had not been notified of the gathering.

Desecration?

The case has been before courts before, but the legal question now is whether the women’s activities constitute desecration.

The participants, who were found out after the father of a buried child discovered a camera at the grave site, allegedly used cat toys with lights to help them communicate with the dead children.

“It is terrible to be confronted with this kind of fact after the loss of a loved one,” prosecutors said. “The way the suspects have dealt with the graves goes against any sense of respect.”

At least 10 relatives have reburied their loved ones in other graves as a result.

Distraught parents

“When people ask me how it feels, I say it feels like rape,” Radia Drost-Laabidi told RTV Utrecht. She and her husband buried two of their daughters at Rusthof. She’s suffered from insomnia ever since and barely visits her daughters’ graves. Now she’s looking for answers. “Why?” she says. “That is my question.”

Only one defendant turned up in court this week, 81-year-old Irene B. Lawyers for the defendants argued that since nothing was damaged or destroyed, there is no desecration.

The court is expected to deliver its verdict next month.

item.title: Bird flu outbreaks prompt national indoor shelter order
item.description:
Bird flu outbreaks prompt national indoor shelter order

October 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Three recent outbreaks of bird flu have led agriculture secretary Silvio Erkens to order farmers to keep their poultry indoors.

Two of the outbreaks occurred in Groningen and one in Noord-Holland. Wild birds, which are currently migrating south, have also been found to carry the disease.

“It is important to limit contact between kept birds and potentially infected wild birds as much as possible,” Erkens told broadcaster NOS. “That way we are doing everything we can to prevent new outbreaks.”

Bird hobbyists don’t have to comply with the order, but they must shield their birds in aviaries or other shelters. All non-essential visitors are also banned from places where birds are kept.

Consumers

While poultry farmers are hard-hit, the price and availability of poultry have remained relatively stable.

“The prices have been high enough for the past couple of months, so they are stable for now,” says Babak Sadeghi, who owns Chris Kip in Amsterdam’s Albert Cuyp Market. “But increased transport and petrol prices have affected suppliers and deliveries.”

Bird flu has also been found in Denmark, Germany, the United Kingdom and other places.

Erkens is pushing for mandatory vaccinations of egg-laying hens against bird flu.

item.title: Mass starfish stranding on Noordwijk beach
item.description:
Mass starfish stranding on Noordwijk beach

October 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Thousands of starfish washed ashore on Tuesday in Noordwijk, creating a visual feast for beachgoers and a literal feast for seagulls.

Experts say the strong winds and currents from recent storms, including the weekend’s storm Boelo, likely dislodged the starfish from the seabed, where they cling to the ground with suction cups, and carried them towards the shore.

Mass starfish strandings are common on Dutch shores, particularly after storms. They wash back out to sea once the water level rises, although many are left for bird prey as they die quickly on land.

The phenomenon, which typically occurs four to eight times a year, is a natural one that doesn’t pose problems for the ecosystem, broadcaster NOS reported. But it could if it occurs more frequently in the future, possibly due to climate change.

Starfish feed on mussels, so if they’re stranded on the shore, the mussel population explodes and weaker ones can survive, leading to disease outbreaks.

item.title: Jetten backpedals on plans to tax the royals
item.description:
Jetten backpedals on plans to tax the royals

October 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten is refusing to act on calls for the royal family to pay taxes, despite his party D66 having actively backed the idea for years.

The Dutch royals receive personal salaries, which is only a fraction of their overall wealth, and plans to tax them on their incomes have been debated by parliament for more than a decade.

The king, for example, will receive roughly €7.5 million from the state next year, of which €1.2 million is personal income and the rest covers staff and running costs. He pays no tax on it. In January 2024 D66 tabled a motion calling on the government to change the constitution so that the royals would pay income tax.

For the first time in history, the motion got two-thirds parliamentary support, with over 100 MPs backing it. But the successive prime ministers Mark Rutte and Dick Schoof both refused to push the plan forward.

Last December D66 also voted for a similar motion by GroenLinks-PvdA (Pro) MP Laura Bromet, asking that royals who receive an allowance pay the same taxes as everyone else.

Now Jetten appears to be doing the same. He told MPs on Wednesday that the yearly debate had become an “unproductive dynamic” and that he wants a broader review of a “future-proof monarchy” instead.

He promised the Christian Democrats (CDA) that it would not lead to a ceremonial monarchy. Ending the exemption would also require a change to the constitution, which exempts the king from tax on his allowance.

Opposition parties are furious at his backpedalling on the issue. “D66 was angry every year that the motions were not implemented. Now the party has a unique opportunity to reflect on the future of the monarchy,” Socialist (SP) MP Sandra Beckerman told NOS. “You would think that you would seize that opportunity.”

Dutch republican group Republiek, which campaigns for the abolition of the monarchy, wrote an open letter to Jetten saying “a large majority of the population indicates time and again in polls that they are in favour of the king paying taxes.”

“For twelve years now, there has been a majority in the House of Representatives in favour of abolishing the tax exemption for the royal family. Time and again, the plans failed during the implementation by the prime ministers. But now you are our prime minister.”

The letter is signed off using the campaign slogan D66 used to come to power in the current coalition: “In your own words: het kan wel” (it’s possible).

MPs will soon vote on a motion from Bromet backing Jetten’s review, and one from Beckerman telling the cabinet to act on the royal tax motions parliament has already passed.
